learn.canDo: Compare threads, processes and async by memory per connection and CPU use, and keep CPU work off the event loop.
learn.why: Concurrency model is the first design decision of a server. Interviewers ask what you would pick for 20,000 connections.
learn.keyIdea: Waiting is free for a CPU and expensive for a stack.

learn.canDo: Explain the GIL, predict when threads help, and choose processes for CPU-bound Python.
learn.why: The GIL question separates people who have profiled from people who have read about threads.
learn.keyIdea: Threads parallelise waiting; processes parallelise computing.

learn.canDo: Spot a read-modify-write race, and fix it with an atomic operation, a lock or by not sharing state.
learn.why: Races are the bugs that appear only under load. Naming the interleaving is the skill.
learn.keyIdea: A read that updates is a write.

learn.canDo: Explain deadlock as a cycle of waiting, and break it with lock ordering, admission limits or timeouts.
learn.why: Deadlocks stall a service at zero CPU. Knowing the four conditions gives you the fix.
learn.keyIdea: Break one link of the cycle.

chapter.story: The service handles load well in testing and then stalls, miscounts or deadlocks in production.
outcomes: Choose a concurrency model for a workload
Know what the GIL does and does not limit
chapter.why: Concurrency bugs depend on timing, so they hide until load finds them. A few rules turn them into design decisions.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can reason about threads, locks and event loops. At work you will recognise a race or a deadlock from the symptoms.
